analysis.one_liner: Lets House candidates run campaigns entirely on public funds instead of private donations.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 35 cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote in any of the three committees it was sent to, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given House candidates a choice: collect a large number of small $5 contributions from voters to qualify, then receive full public funding and agree to take no private money at all. It also would have given clean money candidates free TV and radio time and discounted ad rates, limited what political parties and independent groups could spend against them, barred most taxpayer-funded mass mailings by members running for reelection, and strengthened the Federal Election Commission with new audit and enforcement powers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and candidates without access to wealthy donors or industry money gain a way to run competitive House campaigns funded entirely by small qualifying contributions and public money, while lawmakers who take it would be freed from constant fundraising and barred from most franked election-season mass mailings.

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who collect 1,500 qualifying contributions of exactly $5 from residents of their state can be certified as clean money candidates and receive public campaign funds, with no private contributions allowed beyond limited seed money capped at $35,000 [S3].

Clean money candidates get free broadcast time (30 minutes in primaries, 75 minutes in general elections) and ad rates capped at half the lowest commercial rate, and stations cannot preempt their paid ads [S3].

If outside groups or privately funded opponents outspend a clean money candidate beyond 125% of the public grant, the candidate receives matching public funds, capped at 200% of the original grant [S3].

Members running for reelection would be barred from sending most franked (taxpayer-paid) mass mailings during the primary and general election period, closing a common channel for official self-promotion [S3].

The bill restructures the FEC, mandates electronic filing, expands audit authority including random audits, and gives the commission power to seek court injunctions and expedite election-season complaints [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the grants through a new Treasury fund, and broadcasters bear the cost of free airtime and half-rate ads; wealthy donors, party committees, and privately funded candidates lose the ability to outspend publicly financed opponents.

drawbacks.text: Campaigns would be paid for with federal appropriations to a new House of Representatives Election Fund, a direct taxpayer cost the bill authorizes without a dollar limit [S3].

The bill compels broadcasters to provide free airtime and steep discounts to clean money candidates, a cost imposed on private broadcast companies that drew longstanding First Amendment objections to similar mandates [S3].

Spending limits apply only to candidates who opt in; the matching-fund cushion is capped at 200% of the grant, so a wealthy self-funded or big-money opponent could still swamp a clean money candidate [S3].

The 1,500 qualifying-contribution threshold and elaborate compliance rules (48-hour reports, receipts, remittance deadlines, penalties up to 10 times any improper expenditure) favor candidates with organized field operations and could burden grassroots campaigns [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public cost of financing House campaigns would be modest relative to federal spending, and the bill's own findings argue the system pays for itself by reducing policy outcomes 'skewed' toward big contributors [S3]. The design is voluntary, which limits both its upside (big-money candidates could simply decline) and its constitutional exposure. Its main practical weakness is that matching funds are capped, so it narrows rather than eliminates the money advantage in politics.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and two subcommittees for over a year with no hearing or vote, and the 108th Congress ended without it ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the Clean Money, Clean Elections Act on November 21, 2003, with 29 original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the Committees on House Administration, Energy and Commerce, and Government Reform [S5].
On December 4, 2003, portions were referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet and the Subcommittee on Health; no committee ever reported the bill [S5].
The bill ended the 108th Congress with 35 cosponsors (34 Democrats and 1 Independent) and no floor action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members kept their existing private fundraising system and taxpayer-funded franked mailings, and the donors and broadcasters whose money and airtime dominate House campaigns were spared any new limits. Ordinary voters gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee without any roll-call vote.

industries.note: The bill would replace private campaign contributions in House races that opt into public funding, directly reducing the influence of large donors on elections [S3]. The bill's findings state that concentrated campaign money gives wealthy interests disproportionate access to lawmakers [S3].

Stations would have to give clean money candidates free airtime in prime slots, cap their ad rates at half the lowest commercial rate, and face license jeopardy for denying access [S3]. The industry keeps that revenue only because the bill never advanced.
Party committee spending in any House race with a clean money candidate would be limited to 10% of the public grant, cutting party leverage over House campaigns [S3].
